item.title: Abstracting and Generalising Executors for Modular Game Loops
item.dc:creator: Daniel Torquato
item.description:
At the gameplay level, a game is an ordered set of moments: the player walks a few steps, looks around, approaches a door, a scene plays, something appears in the dark. Each moment has a precondition, a completion condition and side effects on the world. When those moments are scripted directly against each other, the flow is spread across flags, timers and callbacks in many places, and any change in order or content becomes a refactor.

This article describes an architecture that addresses this by treating every moment of the game as an executor: a unit with a uniform lifecycle and an explicit completion event, orchestrated by generic components that know nothing about what each executor does. It covers:

  • The executor contract and its lifecycle;
  • Composition through sequencers and the capabilities a child can expose;
  • Aggregation, readiness barriers and interactions as event sources;
  • Data-driven variation;
  • Extensions of the model (parallelism, selection, cancellation, shared context);
  • A classified segmentation of the project that keeps these boundaries intact.

The examples come from a horror game, but nothing here depends on a genre, an engine or a programming language. Every flow is described as a diagram so that it can be translated to any toolset.

The Problem with Hardcoded Game Loops

Before talking about the solution, it is worth visualising the problem. The most common way to script a sequence of gameplay moments is to let each piece know what comes next.

Every arrow in this diagram is a dependency. The door knows about the cutscene, the cutscene knows about the encounter, and every script reads or writes flags that others left behind. The flow exists, but it exists implicitly, spread across the pieces, and nobody can read it in a single place.

The consequences are predictable:

  • Reordering two moments requires editing every script around them;
  • Reusing a moment in another level drags its neighbours along;
  • A missing object halfway through silently freezes the whole sequence;
  • Testing one moment in isolation is nearly impossible.

What we want is the opposite: pieces that know nothing about each other, and a flow that is described explicitly, in one place, by something whose only job is to run it.

The Executor: The Smallest Unit of Intention

An executor is anything that represents one thing that must happen: wait for the player to walk ten metres, play an animation, spawn a creature, wait until a light is switched off. What makes it an executor is not what it does, but the contract it follows:

  1. It can be started;
  2. While running, it can update itself, every frame or every tick;
  3. At some point it decides it is done and announces that it has finished.

That contract can be modelled as a tiny state machine:

Three states, two transitions that matter. The executor does not know who started it, and it does not know what comes after it. It only knows its own completion condition.

Lifecycle hooks

To avoid every executor reimplementing the same state handling, the base executor owns the state machine and exposes only hooks for the specific behaviour, a classic application of the Template Method pattern1:

The concrete executor never touches the state directly. It prepares what it needs when it starts, measures its own progress while running, calls finish when its condition is met and cleans up afterwards. Everything else is guaranteed by the base.

A few examples of how different moments fit the same shape:

Executor On start On update Completion condition On finish
Walk Show a movement hint Accumulate horizontal distance travelled Distance ≥ N metres Remove the hint
Look around Show a camera hint Accumulate absolute rotation Rotation ≥ N degrees Remove the hint
Get close Place a marker on a target Measure distance to the target Distance ≤ N metres Remove the marker
Cutscene Lock controls, play animation Nothing Animation finished event Restore controls

Notice that the last row has no update logic at all. Its completion comes from another event, which already hints at something important: executors can finish because of time, because of player progress or because something else in the world told them to.

Fail Forward: Executors That Never Deadlock

Games run in messy environments. Objects get renamed, a target is removed from a level, an asset fails to load. In a hardcoded flow, any of these freezes the sequence forever, usually without an error.

Executors can adopt a simple rule: if an executor cannot do its job, it finishes immediately.

The sequence always moves forward. A missing marker means the player does not see a hint, not that the game stops.

TipFail forward or fail stop?

Skipping is the right default for presentation (hints, markers, ambience). For moments that carry state the rest of the game depends on, such as giving the player a key, skipping silently only moves the bug further away. Make the choice explicit per executor and always log the skip, so a broken moment shows up in the logs instead of in a player’s review.

The Sequencer: An Executor of Executors

With a uniform contract in place, the orchestrator becomes almost boringly simple. A sequencer holds an ordered list of executors and runs them one after the other:

The sequencer subscribes to the finished event of the current executor once, starts it and waits. When the event arrives, it moves to the next one. When the list is over, it announces that it has finished.

And that last detail is where the idea becomes powerful: a sequencer follows the same contract as an executor. It can be started and it announces when it is done. So a sequencer can be placed inside another sequencer, exactly like any other executor, which is the Composite pattern2 applied to gameplay flow.

The whole game flow is now a tree you can read. Reordering the tutorial means moving two items in a list. Removing the finale for a demo build means removing one branch. Testing the night sequence means starting that sequencer directly, without playing the tutorial first.

The Contract Is the Interface, Not the Type

There is a subtle decision hidden in the previous section. The sequencer does not ask “is this an executor?”. It asks “can this be started, and does it announce when it finishes?”.

That difference matters because it lets the sequencer orchestrate things that were never designed as executors. A creature that walks a path and announces when it reaches the end, an animation player that announces when a clip ends, a door that announces when it is opened: all of them can join a sequence, as long as they expose the two halves of the contract.

It also gives the sequencer a natural vocabulary for three kinds of children:

  • Blocking executors start and hold the sequence until they finish;
  • Fire-and-forget executors start and let the sequence continue at once, which is a cheap way of running things in parallel (an ambient sound, a flickering light);
  • Non-executors are ignored, so helpers and data can live next to the executors without breaking anything.
NoteExplicit beats implicit, eventually

Checking capabilities at runtime is flexible and fast to prototype with. As the project grows, a formal contract (an interface, a protocol, a trait, whatever your language calls it) catches mistakes earlier, such as a misspelled event name that silently turns a blocking executor into a fire-and-forget one. A good middle ground is to keep the flexible check in the sequencer but log every child it skips or does not wait for.

Waiting for Many: Aggregating Executors

Some moments are not a single action but a group of them. Picture a scene where several figures walk past the player, one after another, and the moment is only over when every one of them has left.

The executor that represents this moment is itself a small orchestrator: it spawns its children at an interval, counts how many finished and only finishes when both counts reach the target.

Two details deserve attention. First, the check happens on both counters: if a child finishes very quickly, before the last one is spawned, the executor must not finish early. Second, the spawn loop checks whether the executor is still running before each spawn, because something else may have finished or interrupted it in the meantime.

Children can also relate to each other. In my case, each spawned figure follows the one in front of it, which turns a list of independent entities into a procession without any extra orchestration.

Readiness Barriers: Making Sure the World Is Ready

Executors assume the world is in place: assets loaded, settings applied, references resolved. When loading is asynchronous, a common source of bugs is an executor starting before what it needs exists.

The same event-driven thinking solves this. Each loader registers itself when it starts, announces when it finishes and a global registry announces when all of them are done.

The most important line in this diagram is the consumer asking before subscribing. Events are not stored: if a consumer subscribes after the loader has already finished, it will wait forever for an event that already happened. This is the late subscriber problem, and the fix is always the same: check the current state first, subscribe only if the result is not there yet.

The other detail is the coalesced check. When several loaders finish in the same frame, the registry schedules a single “are we all done?” check for later in the frame, instead of evaluating it once per loader. The event fires once, at the right moment.

Interactions as Event Sources

So far, executors finish because of their own conditions. The other half of a game is the player doing things: pressing a button, opening a gate, pulling a lever. Those interactions should not call gameplay code directly either. They should become events.

The layering matters. A generic interactable only knows “I was interacted with”. The object that owns it translates that into something meaningful, such as “the gate was opened” or “the lever was pulled”, and only then does gameplay react. Each layer can be reused without the ones above it: the same interactable powers a button, a drawer or a window, and the same opened event can finish an executor, change a light or trigger a sound.

Draggable objects follow the same idea with a slightly richer state machine:

Grabbing an object that is still settling simply starts a new drag, exactly as it would from Idle. Every transition emits a state change event, so a door that slams shut on its own, a locked drawer that rattles or a gate that reaches its limit can all be expressed without the drag logic knowing anything about horror.

Variation Through Data

In a horror game, predictability kills tension. The flow must be readable for the developer and unreadable for the player. The way to get both is to keep the structure fixed and move the variation into data.

Two simple tools go a long way:

  • Profiles: a session description (short, medium or long, for example) that a sequencer reads to decide how many moments to run and how dense they are;
  • Weighted choices: every candidate (a creature, a sound, a texture variation, a line of dialogue) carries a weight, and selection is proportional to it.

Selection walks the list accumulating weights and returns the first candidate whose running sum exceeds the draw, so each candidate wins with a probability proportional to its weight. When every weight is zero, the first candidate is returned instead of failing.

Combined with executors, this turns content design into tuning. A rare scare is a candidate with a low weight. A night that escalates is a profile with denser sequences. None of it requires new code.

Evolving the Engine: What Comes Next

A sequential runner with blocking and fire-and-forget children already covers a surprising amount of a game. But once the contract is stable, the same idea extends naturally, and each extension is just another executor that orchestrates executors:

If this family looks familiar, it is because it converges towards behaviour trees3, with one important difference in intention: here the tree describes the pacing of the game, not the decisions of an agent.

Three improvements to the base contract are worth making before the family grows:

  1. Cancellation. In a horror game, the player can be caught in the middle of anything. Executors need a cancel path, distinct from finish, that cleans up without triggering the next moment. Composites propagate it to their running children.
  2. Reset. An executor that can only run once cannot be reused by a Repeat or replayed after a checkpoint. Resetting state and counters should be part of the contract.
  3. Shared context. Executors frequently need the same references: the player, the main camera, the current session. Looking them up globally from every executor couples them to the world layout. Passing a context (often called a blackboard) from the sequencer down to its children keeps executors portable and makes them trivial to test.

With cancellation in place, the state machine gains one more exit:

Cancellation can arrive at any point before the executor ends, and a reset brings either ending back to the start.

And because every transition is an event, tracing comes almost for free: logging each start, finish, skip and cancel with the executor’s path in the tree gives you a timeline of every session, which is invaluable when a playtester says “it just stopped”.

Classified Segmentation: Organising the Project

An executor architecture only stays modular if the project structure reflects it. When base classes, concrete moments, global services and data all live in the same folder, the boundaries that the code works so hard to keep start to blur.

The approach I settled on is to classify every piece by its nature first, and by its subject second:

A handful of rules make this classification hold over time:

  • One class per folder, named after it, with its visual or scene definition beside it when it has one;
  • Subclasses of a base in the same layer go in a plural folder inside the base’s folder (Loader/Loaders/...), so the family is visible at a glance;
  • Concrete implementations of a core base live in Features, grouped by what they are (Executors/Walk, Executors/Cutscene), never by the level where they first appeared;
  • Helpers that only exist for one class stay in that class’s folder until something else uses them, at which point they earn their own;
  • Dependencies point inwards: Features may depend on Core, Core never depends on Features.

The last rule is the easiest to break and the most important to keep. The moment a core system references a concrete feature, for example the base executor looking up the player, it can no longer be reused in another game or tested without the whole world around it. The shared context described in the previous section is precisely what removes that last dependency.

TipA quick test for your structure

Pick any folder in Core and imagine copying it into a completely different game. If it does not compile, or does not make sense, without something from Features, the boundary has leaked.

Trade-offs

The model is not free, and its costs should be weighed before adopting it:

  • Indirection. The flow is no longer visible in the code of any single piece. Without tooling (a readable tree in the editor, tracing in the logs), “why did this happen now?” becomes harder to answer, not easier;
  • Event chains are harder to debug than calls. A missing or misnamed completion event does not raise an error; it simply never arrives. Logging skipped children and executors that stay Started for too long is the countermeasure;
  • Fail forward hides failures. It keeps the session running, but only logging makes the skip visible, and critical executors should opt out of it;
  • Over-generalisation. Not every behaviour is a moment in a flow. Continuous systems (movement, physics, ambient simulation) belong in the regular update loop, and wrapping them as executors only adds ceremony;
  • Granularity. Executors that are too small turn sequences into long lists of trivial steps; executors that are too large reintroduce the coupling the model was meant to remove. A useful heuristic is one executor per completion condition the designer cares about.

Conclusion

The architecture described here moves the gameplay flow out of the individual pieces and into an explicit, composable structure:

  • A minimal executor contract (start, update, announce the end) with a lifecycle owned by a base and behaviour supplied through hooks;
  • Composition through executors that orchestrate executors, starting with the sequencer and extending to parallel, selector, repeat and decorator variants;
  • Events as the only coupling between pieces, from completion and readiness to player interaction;
  • Data as the source of variation, through profiles and weighted choices;
  • A classified project structure, by nature first and subject second, with dependencies pointing inwards.

The result is a game loop that describes what happens, while each executor decides how.

Footnotes

  1. Gamma, E., Helm, R., Johnson, R. and Vlissides, J. Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, 1994, “Template Method”.↩︎

  2. Ibid., “Composite”. For game-specific variations of these ideas, see Nystrom, R. Game Programming Patterns, 2014, especially the “Update Method”, “Event Queue” and “Service Locator” chapters.↩︎

  3. Behaviour trees are a widely used technique for agent decision-making in games, popularised by their use in large commercial titles in the mid-2000s.↩︎

item.title: Designing Reliable Automation Pipelines for Persistent Game Worlds
item.dc:creator: Daniel Torquato
item.description:
NoteUpdated on November 5, 2026

The reference implementation now also runs Horizon, the community rewrite of Minecraft 26.3 in Rust, next to the official Java server (PR #2, PR #3). This post now covers the new server layer, the Horizon image and how a stop from inside the game is handled.

The previous update (October 22, 2026) was a reliability and security release: most importantly, the GitHub token is no longer embedded in the remote URL, where the original version wrote it to the repository config and to the logs. See the revision history.

Reference Implementation

The complete implementation described throughout this post is publicly available in the following repository:

GitHub Repository
danieltorquatof/minecraft-backup · project page (status and updates)

The project contains the full set of scripts, Docker definitions and utility functions that support the automation flow presented below. The excerpts in this post come from commit 80236c9; reviewing the code directly in the repository can help contextualise the behaviour of each component and illustrate how the pieces integrate in practice.

Key Code Excerpts

Although the full implementation is available in the repository, a few excerpts help illustrate the mechanics behind the automation layer. The example below shows how the autosave routine guards against overlapping runs and then delegates world persistence to a dedicated function that commits the updated data to Git. That function talks to the game through a small server layer, so it works the same with the Java server and with Horizon.

scripts/autosave.sh

View on GitHub

#!/bin/bash
# Periodic backup, run every PERIODIC_INTERVAL minutes while the server is up.
# Can also be run by hand: docker compose exec minecraft /opt/minecraft-backup/scripts/autosave.sh

source /opt/minecraft-backup/utils/saveWorld.sh

LOG_FILE="$LOG_DIR/autosave.log"

exec 9>"$LOCK_FILE"

if ! flock -n 9; then
  log "AUTOSAVE" "Another backup is still running. Skipping."
  exit 0
fi

if ! server_online; then
  log "AUTOSAVE" "Server is not accepting commands yet. Skipping."
  exit 0
fi

log "AUTOSAVE" "Starting execution..."

if ! saveWorld "AUTOSAVE"; then
  log "AUTOSAVE" "Execution failed."
  exit 1
fi

log "AUTOSAVE" "Execution completed."

utils/saveWorld.sh

View on GitHub

# Flushes the world to disk (when the server is running), commits every change and pushes it.
saveWorld() {
  local prefix="$1"
  local online=false

  # ... ensure_repo prepares the repository (omitted)

  if server_online; then
    online=true

    server_cmd 'tellraw @a {"text":"📂 Backup started!","color":"gold"}' >/dev/null

    # Pause automatic saving so region files are not rewritten while they are staged.
    server_cmd save-off >/dev/null
    server_cmd save-all flush >/dev/null
  fi

  local add_status=0
  repo_git add -A || add_status=$?

  if [ "$online" = true ]; then
    server_cmd save-on >/dev/null || log "$prefix" "WARNING: could not re-enable automatic saving."
  fi

  if [ "$add_status" -ne 0 ]; then
    log "$prefix" "ERROR: git add failed."
    return 1
  fi

  if repo_git diff --cached --quiet; then
    log "$prefix" "No changes since the last backup."
  else
    local commit_msg
    commit_msg="$(date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ") - $prefix"

    repo_git commit -q -m "$commit_msg" || return 1
  fi

  # Also sends commits left behind by previous failed pushes.
  if ! repo_git push -q -u origin HEAD; then
    log "$prefix" "ERROR: git push failed."
    # ... warns the players in game (omitted)
    return 1
  fi

  log "$prefix" "Backup successfully pushed."
}

utils/server.sh: one interface, two servers

View on GitHub

SERVER_FLAVOR is set by each Dockerfile. The Java image sends console commands through RCON; Horizon has a local control API (horizon-server cmd), so it needs no RCON at all. Everything above this layer only calls server_cmd and server_online:

# Runs one console command (e.g. `server_cmd save-all flush`). Fails if the server can't be reached.
server_cmd() {
  if is_horizon; then
    horizon cmd "$@"
  else
    rcon "$@"
  fi
}

server_online() {
  if is_horizon; then
    horizon status --json 2>/dev/null | grep -q '"phase":"running"'
  else
    rcon list >/dev/null 2>&1
  fi
}

utils/common.sh: credentials

View on GitHub

The token is handed to Git through an inline credential helper defined in environment variables, so it never reaches the remote URL, a config file or the logs:

export GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0
export GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=3
export GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0="safe.directory"
export GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0="$REPO_DIR"
export GIT_CONFIG_KEY_1="init.defaultBranch"
export GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_1="$GIT_BRANCH"
export GIT_CONFIG_KEY_2="credential.helper"
export GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_2='!f() { test "$1" = get && test -n "$GITHUB_TOKEN" && echo "username=${GITHUB_USER:-x-access-token}" && echo "password=$GITHUB_TOKEN"; }; f'

These sections illustrate the predictable structure that supports periodic and manual world preservation. The underlying model is intentionally minimalistic so the logic remains transparent and easy to debug, while every step reports failures instead of assuming success.

Persistent digital environments demand predictable behaviour. Whether managing corporate infrastructure or personal projects, stability depends on systems that continue to operate even when attention shifts elsewhere. Over time I realised that reliable automation is not only relevant in professional settings. It can also solve surprisingly ordinary problems.

A practical example emerged in my own home. My partner and I often play Minecraft together and our sessions sometimes last several hours. Anyone who has hosted a local or containerised server knows that crashes or unexpected shutdowns can corrupt the world or erase progress. After losing entire builds on more than one occasion I started thinking seriously about how to design a stable and automatic backup mechanism that would remove the risk altogether.

This line of thinking eventually led to a full architecture that integrates Docker, Git and GitHub for continuous world versioning. Although this post uses that implementation as a reference, the focus here is the reasoning that guides the creation of automation pipelines that are reliable, observable and resilient.

Designing the Automation Flow

Before exploring each script it is useful to visualise how the overall workflow operates. The intention was to create a loop that could run indefinitely, independent of the user’s attention.

This diagram reflects the core concept. Every event leads to a deterministic and observable action. World data is always saved, always committed and always pushed, and any step that fails is logged and reported instead of silently ignored.

Understanding the File Structure

The project uses a modular structure that separates concerns and creates predictable behaviours. Each file contributes uniquely to the automation pipeline.

.
├── .github/workflows/ci.yml   # ShellCheck, Hadolint, compose validation, image builds and a Horizon smoke test
├── docker-compose.yml         # Java server (itzg/minecraft-server)
├── docker-compose.horizon.yml # Horizon server (Rust)
├── Dockerfile                 # Java image
├── Dockerfile.horizon         # Horizon image
├── entrypoint.sh              # Startup → periodic loop → graceful shutdown
├── .env.example               # Java settings
├── .env.horizon.example       # Horizon settings
├── scripts
│   ├── autosave.sh            # Periodic backup (can also be run by hand)
│   ├── healthcheck.sh         # Docker health check of the Horizon image
│   ├── init.sh                # Restores/clones the world before the server starts
│   └── shutdown.sh            # Final backup after the server stops
└── utils
    ├── common.sh              # Shared configuration and git helpers
    ├── horizon.sh             # Horizon setup: server.toml, world name, game files
    ├── log.sh                 # Logging to stdout and ./logs
    ├── saveWorld.sh           # Flush → commit → push
    └── server.sh              # Server backend: start, console commands, online check (Java or Horizon)

Each one will be explained individually so the full picture becomes clear.

Container and Image Definitions

docker-compose.yml

Defines how the server is launched. It handles:

  • Port exposure for gameplay only (MC_HOST_PORT, 25565 by default). RCON stays inside the container, since backups are the only thing that uses it;
  • Environment variable loading;
  • Persistence of the Minecraft world and logs;
  • Building the custom image from the local Dockerfile;
  • A three minute stop_grace_period, so Docker does not kill the container while the final backup is being pushed.

Its purpose is to maintain stability across restarts and ensure that all automation scripts remain present inside the container.

docker-compose.horizon.yml does the same for Horizon. It mounts the Minecraft 26.3 game files read-only (Horizon needs files prepared from your own copy of the game, which are never shipped in the image) and allows four minutes to stop, since Horizon may take up to three to save. Both files share ./data, so the same world can move between the two servers, one at a time.

Dockerfile

The Dockerfile extends the “official” image itzg/minecraft-server:java25 (configurable through MC_IMAGE_TAG for older Minecraft versions) then installs all custom scripts under /opt/minecraft-backup. This combination provides the reliability of a well maintained base image while enabling custom behaviour controlled entirely by our own entrypoint.

This duality of stability and customisation supports the idea of predictable infrastructure that can also adapt to specific needs.

Dockerfile.horizon

Horizon publishes an official Dockerfile but no image, so Dockerfile.horizon downloads a pinned, dated nightly release and verifies it against the published SHA256SUMS before installing the same scripts. Pinning matters here: Horizon changes daily, so a new version is tested on a copy of the world before the pin moves. The image runs as UID 1000, like the Java one, and adds a Docker health check.

Core Execution Orchestrator

entrypoint.sh

This script coordinates the lifecycle of the server and backup system.

It performs:

  1. Configuration validation (repository name, token, interval and, for Horizon, the EULA);
  2. Horizon setup, when that image is used (utils/horizon.sh);
  3. Initialisation and startup synchronisation;
  4. Launch of the periodic autosave loop;
  5. Server start through server_start: the itzg start script or horizon-server run;
  6. Graceful shutdown: the server is stopped first, then the final backup runs.

A second diagram helps illustrate this behaviour.

This flow ensures that no world data is lost, regardless of how the container stops. The same final backup also runs when the server stops on its own, for example after /stop in game.

Horizon needed one extra piece here. When the game is stopped from inside (/stop, RCON or horizon-server cmd stop), its supervisor stays up on purpose, waiting for a start that never comes in a container: the container would stay up, autosaves would skip every run and no final backup would be taken. A small watcher (server_watch_stop) ends the supervisor once the game reports stopped twice in a row, after having been up, so the usual shutdown path takes over. Checking twice skips the brief stopped phase a horizon-server restart passes through.

Utility Layers

utils/common.sh

Shared configuration used by every script: the Git identity (commits fail without a committer), the credential helper shown above and a function that runs Git as the same user as the server, so no world file ends up owned by root.

utils/server.sh

The server backend shown in the excerpts: how to start the server, send it console commands and tell whether it is up, for either flavour. It also holds the Horizon stop watcher.

utils/horizon.sh

Runs only on the Horizon image, before the world is restored. It writes server.toml on the first start, always sets the world name to the backup repository name, turns off Horizon’s own zip backups (they also pause saving and would collide with the Git ones) and checks that the prepared game files are present, stopping the container with a clear message when they are not.

utils/log.sh

A lightweight logger that standardises how each script communicates events. Every log entry includes a timestamp and prefix and goes both to docker compose logs and to persistent storage, so it survives container recreation. This improves verification and troubleshooting.

utils/saveWorld.sh

The most responsibilities in the automation pipeline concentrate here. It performs:

  • In game world flush through the server layer (RCON on Java, the control API on Horizon), with automatic saving paused while files are staged
  • Git staging and committing (only when something changed)
  • Push synchronisation with GitHub, including commits left behind by earlier failed pushes
  • Messaging for both users and logs

It represents the core reliability mechanism. If this script functions correctly, every world state becomes recoverable.

Lifecycle Scripts

scripts/init.sh

Executed only during startup. It validates the remote repository, checks whether it exists and whether it is empty. It clones the repository, fast-forwards an existing clone or prepares a new one so the world directory becomes fully managed by Git. A local world without history is moved aside instead of being overwritten. This step prevents drift between the running server and the stored history.

scripts/autosave.sh

Runs periodically based on the interval defined in the environment variables. It skips the run when another backup is still in progress or the server is not ready yet, and otherwise calls saveWorld.sh. These periodic commits create a complete backup timeline.

scripts/shutdown.sh

Triggered after the server has stopped, whether by docker compose stop, by the game itself or, on Horizon, by the stop watcher. It waits for any backup still in progress and calls saveWorld.sh so the final server state is stored safely. Because the server has already flushed the world to disk, this prevents data corruption and makes the server restart friendly regardless of how the container was stopped.

Environment Templates and Management

.env.example and .env.horizon.example

Guide the user in defining:

  • GitHub repository credentials (a fine-grained token limited to the backup repository is enough)
  • Minecraft server settings and the base image tag
  • Backup intervals and an optional Git remote other than GitHub
  • Metadata for commits
  • For Horizon: the EULA, where the prepared game files are and first-start settings such as the seed and whitelist

This separation of configuration strengthens clarity and reduces accidental misconfiguration, and the entrypoint refuses to start with an invalid one.

Why This Matters

Although the technical implementation is interesting, the motivation emerged from a real problem. Playing Minecraft with my partner is one of our favourite activities and losing progress due to corruption or abrupt shutdowns was frustrating. Manual backups were easy to forget and relying on memory alone was not sustainable.

Creating an infrastructure that handles backups automatically removed the cognitive load entirely. It also ensured that every session became safe. The system evolved from a personal inconvenience into an elegant example of how automation thinking can improve both professional and personal digital environments.

This project demonstrates that reliable systems do not appear spontaneously. They are built through reasoning, testing and iteration. The first version already worked for everyday use, yet running it for months revealed failures that only appear over time: commits that failed without a committer identity, a token that leaked into the logs, a final backup racing against the server’s own shutdown. Adding a second server later was mostly a matter of putting a small interface where the code used to call RCON directly, and testing it against the real thing exposed the one behaviour no documentation mentioned: a game that stops while its supervisor keeps running. Whether used for game worlds, business processes or experimental environments, the principles remain consistent: predictable automation, clear observability and robust fallback mechanisms.

Final Considerations

Constructing automation flows like this establishes a foundation for trust in any persistent system. Once the structure works without supervision, users are free to focus on the experience rather than maintenance. In my case it allowed long sessions of building and exploration with my partner to continue without disruption.

I hope this explanation clarifies not only what the system does, but also how it was structured and why the reasoning behind it led to a reliable design.

Revision history

  • November 5, 2026: Added Horizon (Rust) support to the reference implementation (PR #2, PR #3): server layer (utils/server.sh) in the excerpts, Horizon image and compose file, Horizon setup and the in-game stop watcher.
  • October 22, 2026: Updated for the reliability and security release of the reference implementation (PR #1): new code excerpts, credential handling, graceful shutdown, consistent snapshots, Java 25 image and CI.
  • December 4, 2025: First published.

item.title: Minecraft Backup
item.dc:creator: Daniel Torquato
item.description:
Overview

Minecraft Backup wraps a Minecraft server with a custom entrypoint that treats the world folder as a Git repository. It ships two images: one built on the official itzg/minecraft-server Java image, and one running Horizon, the community rewrite of Minecraft 26.3 in Rust. The world is restored from GitHub when the container starts, committed and pushed at a fixed interval while people play, and backed up one last time after the server stops cleanly, so a world can always be recovered, moved to another machine or rolled back to an earlier commit.

  • Periodic backups: a Git commit every PERIODIC_INTERVAL minutes, created only when something changed.
  • Consistent snapshots: automatic saving is paused (save-off / save-all flush) while files are staged.
  • Graceful shutdown: the server stops first, then the final backup is committed and pushed.
  • Safe credentials: the GitHub token stays in memory, never in the remote URL, the repository config or the logs.
  • Any Git remote: GitHub by default, or GitLab, Gitea or a bare repository through GIT_REMOTE_URL.
  • Java or Horizon (Rust): both servers use the vanilla world format, so the same backup repository can move from one to the other.
  • Compatible with the official image: every itzg/minecraft-server variable still works on the Java image.

Quick start

git clone https://github.com/danieltorquatof/minecraft-backup.git
cd minecraft-backup
cp .env.example .env   # set GITHUB_USER, GITHUB_TOKEN and REPO_NAME
docker compose up -d --build

For Horizon, prepare the Minecraft 26.3 game files from your own copy of the game with the Horizon launcher, then:

cp .env.horizon.example .env   # backup variables + HORIZON_EULA and HORIZON_RESOURCES_DIR
docker compose -f docker-compose.horizon.yml up -d --build

The README covers the token permissions, every variable, the Horizon setup and how to restore an older backup.

Updates

Date Update
2026-11-05 Horizon (Rust) support (PR #2, PR #3): a second image runs a pinned, checksum-verified Horizon release with the same Git backups. Console commands go through Horizon’s local control API instead of RCON, the world name and game files are set up on start, and stopping the game from inside (/stop) now ends the container with a final backup, as on the Java server. CI builds both images and smoke-tests Horizon.
2026-10-22 Reliability and security release (PR #1): backup commits no longer fail silently, graceful shutdown before the final backup, token removed from remote URLs and logs, consistent snapshots with backup locking, safer handling of empty or diverged remotes, RCON no longer published, Java 25 base image and CI (ShellCheck, Hadolint, compose validation, image build).
2025-12-04 Initial release: periodic Git backups to GitHub, restore on startup and backup on shutdown.

A practical exploration of reasoning, architecture and stable backup mechanisms

This post presents the reasoning process and technical decisions that led to the creation of a reliable backup and automation workflow for persistent game servers, including a real use case related to maintaining stable Minecraft sessions at home.

item.title: Step by step guide on how to ruin your company and your team with AI
item.dc:creator: Daniel Torquato
item.description:
It’s pretty easy to keep a team organized with a well-defined workflow, right?

But if you want to showcase your incompetence or simply watch everything go up in flames, this post is for you!

Already in a leadership position and ready to swim against the tide? Here are some tips to quickly turn everything upside down, bringing chaos and demotivation as fast as possible to everyone relying on your work.

And the best part:

  • Without much effort;
  • Reducing your workload;
  • And with the most groundbreaking tool of the moment1!

To better understand where you can fail and make it blatantly obvious to everyone, let’s break down the following workflow I’ve created:

See how easy it is to visualize how simple processes can trigger a chain of problems that will inevitably lead to your undeniable exclusion and eventual termination?

Maybe you felt personally attacked by how this topic was introduced.

If so, part of that is due to the Psychological Reactance phenomenon2 combined with elements of Reverse Psychology3.

By deliberately exaggerating the impact of the indiscriminate use of this miraculous tool4 — framing as “correct” something that is generally frowned upon—you, as the likely target audience, are naturally inclined to resist and deny it. After all, how hard is it to admit that what currently makes you a professional could easily be the nightmare of many of your colleagues? Or worse, that you could be replaced by an inanimate tool?

This negative reaction from this category of workers is expected since they are already dependent on this enabler5, and the idea that it might be harmful—not just to them but to everyone around them—doesn’t fit the short-term results they have experienced so far.

From a broader perspective, part of the blame may not be entirely yours but rather the fault of those who sold you the idea that this tool6 is the solution to all your monotonous tasks. However, the lack of supervision and limitation of its use will always lead to its application in a wide range of areas—without proper impact assessment and consideration of consequences—far beyond the monotonous tasks it was originally designed for7.

Currently, most AI models are in constant development and far from their peak, with limitations and flaws that are imperceptible at first glance. This is because their entire functioning is designed to socially please the user, meaning they are structured in a way that prevents you from feeling like you’re facing incorrect or nonsensical information.

Not convinced? Maybe you’re still caught in Automation Bias8. To open your eyes, here are some phenomena that might be happening to you daily without you even realizing it:

  • Hallucinations9, where the tool10 generates responses that, while appearing coherent, have no real basis, being merely a statistical approximation11 of what would best fit the given context. This happens due to the lack of logical reasoning in these products12, making some responses essentially just “educated guesses.”
  • Context Window13, which limits the amount of information the tool14 can process at once, meaning that it often fails to grasp the full context of a situation, leading to responses that don’t align with reality. This becomes even more concerning as there is no explicit indication of what is or isn’t discarded by the tool15.

In conclusion, the use of AI tools in corporate environments should be approached with caution and always under the supervision of a qualified professional. After all, no tool can replace critical thinking and assertive decision-making—no matter how convincing or convenient it may seem.

I hope this reading has helped you open your eyes to the dangers of so-called “miracle” automation tools, both for current AI and for future technologies that may emerge.

TipRemember

The problem is never the tool itself, but how it is used!
